title: Pinchas ben Guvta of Ariach
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: An incident concerning him is cited in [Sifrei Bamidbar, Balak 131:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Sifrei_Bamidbar.131.2). He was rolling barrels when the spirit of Peor came to him. He brandished the spit against the spirit, which fled and went away. The spirit returned to him a second time at night and asked: “Why are you cursing me?” He replied: “I will not curse you again from now on.”[^1] In the checked edition of the [Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin, chapter Chelek, halakhah 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sanhedrin.10.2.16), the name reads “Menahem of Gufta-Ariach.”[^2]

notes.text: Hyman labels the first source ספרא בלק, retained in the source archive. The matching passage is found in Sifrei Bamidbar 131:2 (Wikisource edition), with Pinchas ben Guvta of Ariach and the same barrel/spit incident. The checked Yerushalmi likewise has the man take the spit and stand against the spirit. Rabbi Shraga Silverstein’s translation of the Sifrei explicitly makes the spirit flee and return, clarifying the actors adopted here. The Penei Moshe commentary (Piotrków, 1898–1900) explains that the man was occupied with his work and the spirit came to provoke him for cursing it. Guggenheimer calls the Yerushalmi story fragmentary; these witnesses support the immediate narrative reading, not a reconstructed fuller story or a newly checked Hyman printing.

Hyman reports the Yerushalmi variant as מנחם איש נופתה אריה. The checked Guggenheimer Hebrew edition instead reads מְנַחֵם אִישׁ גּוּפְתָּה אָרִיחַ, and its English translation gives “Menaḥem from Guvta-Ariaḥ.” The body follows that explicitly named edition, while preserving Hyman’s different reported form here. This is a comparison of textual readings, not an authority identity join or a claim that the native printed letters have been reread. ה״ב is halakhah 2; the modern segment locator is 10:2:16.
